correctness.rationale: The inclusion indicators for i.i.d. draws give the stated expectations via the probability (1-p_i)^m of missing species i. P strictly majorizes Q (strict first partial sum, equal second and total), and x ↦ (1-x)^m is strictly convex on (0,1) when m>1, yielding strict size order for all real m>1. Both R and C strictly increase and are continuous. Independently verified C_Q(2)<C_P(2)<C_Q(3), R_Q(2)>R_P(2), C_Q(7)<C_P(11)<C_Q(8), and R_Q(8)<R_P(11), with both P coverage levels above the two one-individual bases. Therefore Q wins at the first common coverage and P at the second; continuity forces a crossing. The proof uses only the integer brackets and strict monotonicity of the interpolants, so applies both to the real-power extension and to straight segments between integer-effort points. The result refutes the unrestricted continuous-curve implication of Appendix G, G1, and its G3 crossing-count claim under these conventions. It is not a claim that there are two un-interpolated integer pairs with exactly equal expected coverage, nor a statement about estimated rarefaction curves.

value.rationale: A three-species example with all masses positive and equal true richness shows that the choice of effort standard can reverse qualitative expected rankings despite strict all-effort size dominance. It pinpoints a false universal assertion in the theoretical foundation of coverage standardization, and the polygonal check makes it useful without appealing to fractional sampling. It says nothing about the validity of coverage standardization for other purposes.
